video_title: We're Not Going Back to January 2026 with Art Berman | TGS 237
gist: Petroleum geologist Art Berman tells Nate Hagens (recorded Sept 19, 2026) that the Hormuz disruption hurt less than feared only because of one-off buffers (SPR draws, bypass pipelines, a suspicious 4.5m b/d drop in Chinese imports) that are now exhausted, with ~14m b/d of Gulf output shut in and 5-20% of it possibly never recovering. He argues refining underinvestment, a $200+ diesel-equivalent price, LNG/fertilizer stress, and the US failure to guarantee maritime trade mean the world is not going back to pre-war conditions.

insights.claim: Art Berman says the Strait of Hormuz disruption cost the world only about 10 million barrels/day instead of the feared ~20 million because bypass pipelines, strategic petroleum reserve draws and an unexplained ~4.5 million b/d cut in Chinese crude imports absorbed the blow.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: The muted price reaction so far reflects one-off buffers, not real supply resilience; don't extrapolate the calm.
insights.quote: instead of losing 20 million barrels a day, we ended up only losing maybe 10 million barrels a day

insights.claim: Berman admits he and most analysts he respects were wrong in expecting Hormuz to be an immediate 'heart attack' for the world economy; he got diesel and product prices right but underestimated how well the system adapted.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Calibrate doomer forecasts on timing: the adaptation lag can be months, but the bill still comes due.
insights.quote: a trip to the emergency room turned out to be, uh, you know, a trip to the drugstore

insights.claim: Berman believes the system's buffers are already depleted and have been for weeks; asked whether the 'emergency room' is coming, he says the car is being warmed up now.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Expect the next supply disruption to transmit directly to prices/demand destruction with little cushion.
insights.quote: We're getting the car warmed up right now

insights.claim: The attack on Saudi Aramco's East-West pipeline that bypasses the Persian Gulf removed roughly 4-5 million b/d of bypass capacity and in Berman's view 'tied a bow' around the fact that buffers are exhausted.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Bypass infrastructure is itself a drone target; Gulf export capacity should be treated as fragile, not substitutable.

insights.claim: US SPR is at 40-50-year lows; EIA abruptly pulled its SPR data three or four weeks before the interview and posted a revision notice, and Berman says no one, including DOE, knows the level at which the caverns run into operational trouble.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Official SPR data is less reliable now; the US backstop may be smaller than headline volumes suggest.

insights.claim: SPR withdrawal rates peaked in June at millions of barrels per week and have slowed to a couple hundred thousand barrels per week, which Berman says is not good news because rates matter more to markets than absolute volumes.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: A slowing SPR release removes a marginal supply source just as other buffers thin out.
insights.quote: the rates are always more important, certainly for, well, for me, but also for markets

insights.claim: About 14 million b/d of Persian Gulf production is actually shut in at the wellhead, not just stranded in storage, which Berman calls an unprecedented 'n equals one experiment'.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Reservoir-level shut-ins create restart risk that headline 'peace deal' trades will ignore.
insights.quote: 14 million barrels a day of Persian Gulf production is shut in

insights.claim: Official energy data lags badly: the IEA's latest oil market report discusses April and May numbers because those are the only ones it is confident in, which Berman says are a lifetime ago given current conditions.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Markets keyed to agency balances are trading stale information; private real-time indicators carry edge.

insights.claim: Berman finds it very hard to believe China made a policy choice to cut 4 million b/d of crude imports and thinks it is largely a hidden demand-destruction story, a feature of every past oil shock.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Treat China's import drop as a growth warning signal, not a strategic stockpile play; bearish read for Chinese industrial demand.
insights.quote: I just have a very difficult time believing that China made a policy decision to cut 4 million barrels of crude imports a day

insights.claim: With global inventories thin, minimal SPR support and 10+ million b/d still missing from the Middle East, both host and guest agree the outcome is both much higher prices and demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Position for simultaneous price spikes and regional demand collapse, unevenly distributed by import dependence.
insights.quote: And it's both. It's absolutely both.

themes.theme: Restart risk and the new price floor

insights.claim: Berman estimates that 5% to 15-20% of shut-in Persian Gulf production will never return to pre-shut-in levels once turned back on, because restoring flow through microscopic rock pore pathways is among the riskiest operations in the industry.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Permanent loss of several million b/d of capacity would structurally tighten oil markets even after peace.
insights.quote: probably five to 15 or 20% of that production, once it's turned back on, will never come back to levels that it was before

insights.claim: Even in the best case, restoring reservoir pressures on shut-in Gulf fields will take weeks to months, far longer than political timelines assume.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Fade 'ceasefire = immediate supply return' rallies in tanker/oil-short trades.

insights.claim: Even if peace breaks out, normalization of Persian Gulf shipping would take months because tanker owners, insurers and crews must accept the risk, and mines of unknown number remain in channels — a tanker hit a mine the week before the interview.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Shipping insurance and tanker rates stay elevated well after any diplomatic deal.
insights.quote: nobody knows how many mines are, are, are in these shipping channels. Probably not the Iranians either.

insights.claim: Nate Hagens argues that, barring an economic depression, current oil and refined-product prices are the new floor rather than the ceiling, and that a stone-like drop in gasoline prices would itself signal a deep recession.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Use any sharp gasoline price collapse as a recession indicator rather than relief.
insights.quote: these are now the new floors for oil and refined product, not the ceiling going forward

insights.claim: Hagens dismisses President Trump's claim that gasoline prices will 'drop like a stone' after the election and the war ends as Orwellian, because too many parts of the supply system have been upset.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Political price targets are not achievable through diplomacy alone; don't trade on them.

insights.claim: Berman notes that after the early-1980s shock oil hit roughly $145/bbl in today's dollars, then averaged about $45 from 1986 to the end of the 1990s because much of the developing world fell into a major recession.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Historical template: price spike followed by a long low-price era driven by demand collapse, not supply recovery.

insights.claim: Berman says the 1979-81 shock (Iran-Iraq War, Islamic Revolution) was similar to today's as a share of supply and its effects on economy, prices and production lasted 15 years.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Investors should model a multi-year regime, not a temporary 'shock' that mean-reverts in quarters.
insights.quote: The effects of that on the global economy and on oil prices and on oil production lasted 15 years.

insights.claim: Berman predicts a price run-up, then uneven demand destruction, then eventually a version of the post-1970s decade-and-a-half of global recession — but warns it will be worse than that template because today's economy is far larger and more complex.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Long-horizon bear case for global growth and cyclicals; eventual low oil prices would come via depression.
insights.quote: This is not gonna play like that movie did

insights.claim: Unlike the 1980s, there is no easy supply response: then high prices spurred a deepwater discovery wave and the Soviet collapse opened huge reserves; today proved reserves and undiscovered potential are far smaller relative to a roughly doubled population.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Don't expect a 1980s-style supply wave to cap prices; the recovery path is demand-led.

themes.theme: Refining bottleneck and the diesel premium

insights.claim: Hagens cites the diesel-equivalent price of oil at over $200/bbl, and around $240 in China, more than double crude prices.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: The crisis is concentrated in middle distillates; crack spreads and refiners are where the dislocation lives.

insights.claim: Berman says refinery capacity was already restricted before the war due to under-investment; the only notable new refinery in recent years is Dangote in Nigeria.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Refining capacity scarcity is structural; existing complex refiners with heavy-crude capability hold pricing power.
insights.quote: The only new refinery I know of that's been built in recent years is Dangote in Nigeria

insights.claim: Twenty years of peak-oil-demand and 'twilight industry' messaging have deterred 30-40-year capital commitments to deepwater, Arctic exploration and especially new refineries, making today's investment climate completely different from the early 1980s.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Underinvestment is self-reinforcing; capex discipline means supply can't respond to price, sustaining upstream/refining margins.
insights.quote: Who wants to put their money into something like that? No one does.

insights.claim: US light shale oil is excellent for gasoline but lacks heavy components needed for diesel, so the US depends on heavy crude imports — about 4 million b/d from Canada — for diesel, jet fuel and kerosene.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Canadian heavy crude is strategically critical; US-Canada trade friction is a direct diesel-supply risk.
insights.quote: If, if the world ran on gasoline, the United States would be the king.

insights.claim: Berman says US participation in a Venezuela oil venture is mostly a talking point: Venezuelan heavy crude cannot make gasoline, and new barrels arrive far beyond consumers' time horizon.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Discount Venezuela headlines as a near-term gasoline price fix; relevance is long-dated and diesel-specific.

insights.claim: Workarounds like ship-to-ship transfers between tankers inside and outside the Gulf, which Energy Secretary Chris Wright touts as doubling Gulf exports, carry added cost, time, risk and liability.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Higher logistics friction is a persistent tax embedded in delivered oil prices.
insights.quote: But it isn't free. It comes with cost.

insights.claim: Oil rerouted via the Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea and north through Suez ends up in the Mediterranean, serving the Atlantic Basin rather than Asia, leaving 'the whole oil system in the wrong place at the wrong time'.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Watch regional spreads: Asian product premiums vs Atlantic Basin; Asia bears disproportionate shortage.
insights.quote: now you've got the, the whole oil system in the wrong place at the wrong time

insights.claim: Berman contrasts the globalized 1980s energy system with today's fragmented one, in which China and Russia are actively reorganizing energy and currency flows and wars in Ukraine and Iran add volatility.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Fragmentation raises risk premia and reduces the market's ability to rebalance efficiently.

insights.claim: Hagens frames a 'biophysical gauntlet': oil prices must be high enough to spur next-generation supply investment yet low enough for debt-laden economies and strapped consumers, and wartime volatility makes long-cycle commitments harder.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: The investable price band may have no overlap now, implying chronic underinvestment and demand destruction together.

insights.claim: Hagens and Berman expect both producers and importers to build national energy buffers and more state capitalism or resource nationalism, echoing Jeff Currie's call for state-funded refining and exploration when private capital won't invest.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: State-directed capex and stockpiling could become a new demand source and change how markets clear.

themes.theme: Gas, LNG and the food chain

insights.claim: Berman says the natural gas story is every bit as urgent as oil: LNG-dependent Bangladesh and Pakistan, plus Syria, face strident protests over prices, and governments are promising subsidies to avert unrest.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: EM sovereign/fiscal stress and political risk in LNG importers; subsidy burdens widen deficits.
insights.quote: The natural gas story is every bit as urgent as the oil story.

insights.claim: Europe is paying about $25 per million BTU for gas versus under $3 in the US, and Volkswagen is shutting German production plants partly as a result.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Massive US-Europe energy cost gap accelerates European deindustrialization and favors US energy-intensive industry.

insights.claim: Europe swapped Russian pipeline-gas dependence for costly imported LNG from the US and Qatar; with Qatari LNG now unavailable, it faces renewed scarcity.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: US LNG exporters gain leverage; European industrials and utilities stay under pressure.

insights.claim: Unlike oil, LNG can't be rerouted with ship-to-ship transfers because it must stay super-cooled, so Qatari gas trapped behind Hormuz stays trapped.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: LNG markets lack oil's workaround flexibility; gas disruptions are stickier than crude disruptions.

insights.claim: Hagens reports hearing from multiple sources of a caloric shortfall in 2028 if not 2027, driven by lagged fertilizer (urea, ammonia) shortfalls through Gulf chokepoints, a European drought preventing sowing, an incoming Super El Niño and closed Ukrainian/Russian grain ports.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Second-order agricultural commodity and food-inflation risk with a one-to-two season lag.
insights.quote: there's going to be a caloric shortfall in 2028, if not 2027

themes.theme: Energy growth rate and the technology myth

insights.claim: Berman argues the global economy depends on increasing energy flows yet the rate of growth in energy supply has been declining since the late 1960s; the Iran war 'ripped the Band-Aid off' that mismatch.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Structural headwind to long-run GDP growth assumptions embedded in equity valuations.

insights.claim: Oil demand used to grow about 2 million b/d per year and now grows about 1 million b/d, with this year and next far less, and maintaining today's system requires more energy than the entire system plus growth did 40-50 years ago.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Overhead energy needs rise with scale, so slowing supply growth bites harder than headline volumes suggest.

insights.claim: Berman says there has never been an energy transition, only energy additions: biomass, coal, oil, gas, hydro and nuclear have all been layered on with none decreasing, so the investment world's substitution mindset has no historical precedent.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Bet on 'and' not 'or': fossil demand persists alongside renewables; substitution-based valuations are fragile.
insights.quote: We never transitioned from anything to anything.

insights.claim: Berman calls running the current global economy for 8.2 billion people on anything other than mainly fossil fuels, for now, a fantasy; renewables have different capabilities and are adding to rather than replacing the system.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Supports long-duration fossil fuel demand even under aggressive renewables build-out.

insights.claim: Hagens notes China expects a massive coal gigawatt expansion in 2027, a sign that the shock is driving a return to coal alongside electrification.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Coal demand tailwind; energy security trumps decarbonization targets.

insights.claim: Berman says sophisticated fund managers share a 'technology always comes through' mythology, ignoring that every year of tech progress was backed by more energy and that technologies hit diminishing returns with energy, ecological and human costs.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Consensus tech optimism (AI, markets near highs) underprices energy constraints.
insights.quote: The technology always comes through.

insights.claim: Berman says US shale is no longer viewed as able to make a difference: the breakthrough hype has gone quiet for about a year, and Hagens adds that every shale play except perhaps the Permian has peaked.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: No US shale cavalry; shale equities are cash-flow stories, not growth stories, and US output may plateau.
insights.quote: It's no longer viewed as having the potential to make a difference.

insights.claim: Hagens connects 5% five- and 10-year Treasury yields, $40 trillion of US debt, no new refineries, peaked shale, eroding Middle East security architecture and costly energy abroad into a risk-prone outlook for the next 18 months, against narrow-boundary 'AI is here, stocks are up' complacency.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Macro-energy bear case vs. equity optimism; a potential catalyst for repricing risk assets within 18 months.

insights.claim: Hagens suspects EIA and IEA forecasts carry built-in optimism bias; Berman questions EIA's projection of 112 million b/d of supply a year out, saying he'd love to ask how that is possible.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Agency supply forecasts likely overstate recovery; consensus balances may be too loose.
insights.quote: We'll be at 112 million barrels a day is what EIA says.

themes.theme: End of US maritime guarantee and resource competition

insights.claim: Berman argues the post-WWII trade architecture rests on the US guaranteeing free maritime trade in exchange for reserve-currency status, and that the US has 'abjectly failed' that role in the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Long-run risk to dollar hegemony and US power projection; supports hedges like gold and non-USD settlement themes.
insights.quote: We have, we have abjectly failed, and nobody's talking about that, but everybody knows it

insights.claim: Gulf countries are politely pursuing other security deals because they no longer expect US protection, with world-changing implications for the balance of power.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Watch Gulf realignment toward China/others; petro-flow direction and currency of settlement may shift.

insights.claim: Berman says the petrodollar has effectively not existed for about 20 years; the relevant system is the eurodollar credit system, still largely an American monopoly, which faces new uncertainty as US performance fails the grand bargain.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Dollar risk channel runs through eurodollar credit confidence rather than oil invoicing per se.

insights.claim: Berman expects far more intense, open competition for remaining critical resources and says China and Russia are well ahead of the West, with China having spent decades securing access to resources and refining supply chains from oil to silver and every mineral.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Critical minerals and resource security are strategic; Western catch-up policy (Trump administration critical-minerals push) is a theme to own.
insights.quote: we don't have an infinite pot of, of resources, and the winner, such as they might be, are the ones that have the most access to it

insights.claim: Berman says the world is not going back to January 2026 across oil, LNG, fertilizer, food, geopolitics, currency and finance, though he avoids sounding apocalyptic.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Regime change: reprice assets for structurally higher energy/security risk rather than mean reversion.
insights.quote: We are not going back to January 2026

insights.claim: What would change Berman's mind: authentic US talks with the opposition, countries refilling strategic reserves, oil moving through Hormuz and the Red Sea without coercive security, and above all shut-in production restarting and the forecast agency barrels actually showing up — he assigns these low probability.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Concrete checklist of bullish-supply signposts to monitor.

insights.claim: Berman's key tracking advice: ignore the daily noise of 7 vs 9 million b/d through Hormuz and watch how much shut-in production is restarted and recovering, and how the world responds to much higher diesel and jet fuel prices.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Focus models on restart recovery rates and distillate demand destruction, not transit counts.
insights.quote: don't get distracted by the little stuff
